authoritativeText:
The preceding lesson used small loops and magnetic needles to determine field direction, showing that the quantity describing a magnetic field must be a vector.
Direction alone is not enough: how strong is the field, and how can a measurement determine this magnitude?

Recall an electrostatic field: divide the force on a small test charge by the amount of that charge to obtain the electric field strength.
Provided the test charge does not appreciably disturb the original field, this ratio is not set by the test-charge amount and can describe the field at its location.
The object used for measurement and the field being measured are different things.

A small current-carrying loop can probe a magnetic field, but it responds differently from a test point charge.
If the external magnetic field is uniform over the whole loop, adding the magnetic forces on all parts of the closed loop gives zero net force.
These magnetic forces therefore do not accelerate the center of mass in any direction; zero net force does not mean that every part is force-free.

Even with zero net force, magnetic forces can produce a torque that turns the loop.
In a uniform external field, the magnetic torque on a planar loop depends on its orientation, enclosed area, and current.
Orientation means the direction in which the loop plane faces; when these quantities are fixed, the plane boundary need not have one particular shape.

The textbook uses a single turn of wire carrying current $I$ to investigate the torque.
Treat the magnetic field as uniform over the loop: when the loop plane is perpendicular to the line joining the magnet poles, the orientation in Figure 250 has zero magnetic torque.
For the current direction illustrated, forces on individual parts can stretch the loop without producing a net turning torque.
At this orientation, the elastic suspension does not need to be twisted to balance a magnetic torque.

Turn the loop away from its stable orientation and pass current through it: a magnetic torque tends to turn it back.
If it is free to turn and gradually settles, it returns to the stable orientation in Figure 250.
This is a tendency to rotate, not an assertion that the loop instantly stops without oscillating.

To hold a loop at an angle away from its stable orientation, a torque must oppose the magnetic torque.
Figure 251 uses the elastic twisting of the suspension to provide this balance.

Turn the loop so its plane is perpendicular to the loop plane in Figure 250: the magnetic field direction then lies within the loop plane, while the loop normal is perpendicular to the field.
With other conditions unchanged, the magnetic torque magnitude is now greatest, as in Figure 252.
The textbook holds this orientation by twisting an elastic suspension; within the elastic measurement range being considered, it corresponds to the greatest balancing twist.

For a single-turn planar loop in the same uniform external field, the maximum torque $M_{\text{max}}$ is proportional to enclosed area $S$ times current $I$.
The relation is
$M_{\text{max}}\propto IS.$
When current or area changes, the field must still be approximately uniform over the loop.

This experimental relation lets us separate the field being measured from the probe-loop current and area.
For a single-turn loop, divide the maximum torque by the product of current and area:
$\frac{M_{\text{max}}}{IS}=B$.
This is Equation $(11-1)$ in the textbook, and it gives the magnitude of the magnetic flux density vector.
If a small loop does not appreciably disturb the field and the external field is approximately uniform over it, this ratio describes the field rather than a property belonging to one particular loop; a coil with multiple turns must also account for its number of turns.

Knowing the magnitude and direction of the magnetic flux density vector $\vec B$ at each point describes the magnetic field across those locations.
The vector can vary from place to place, so a measurement at one point does not replace a description of the whole field.

Electric field strength is represented by the vector $\vec E$, while magnetic flux density is represented by the vector $\vec B$.
Both are vectors, but their definitions and their actions on probe objects are different.

The SI unit can be illustrated with a single-turn loop: current 1 ampere, enclosed area 1 m$^2$, and maximum magnetic torque $M_{\text{max}}=1$ newton-meter correspond to one unit of magnetic flux density.
Putting the units into the ratio of maximum torque to current times area gives
$1\text{ unit of magnetic flux density}=1\frac{\text{N}\cdot\text{m}}{\text{A}\cdot\text{m}^2}=1\frac{\text{N}}{\text{A}\cdot\text{m}}.$
The area is the area enclosed by the loop, not the cross-sectional area of the wire material.

The SI unit of magnetic flux density is called the tesla.
The name comes from the surname of the scientist Tesla; it names a unit of a physical quantity, not a kind of coil or magnet.

routing.reason: Apparatus and vector/loop relationships require exact deterministic geometry; no natural artwork or paid generation is needed.
